content: 1. Peter JG and colleagues conducted a study to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of a urine-based lipoarabinomannan (LAM) strip test for tuberculosis (TB) detection in HIV-infected hospitalized patients. The findings were published in the European Respiratory Journal in 2012. 2. Another study by Peter JG and collaborators assessed the impact of point-of-care urine-based LAM testing on mortality rates among HIV-positive inpatients. This pragmatic, multicountry, open-label, randomized controlled trial was published in The Lancet in 2016. 3. The lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay (LF-LAM) has been recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for diagnosing active tuberculosis in individuals living with HIV. This policy update is available on the WHO website. 4. WHO has consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, particularly focusing on drug-resistant TB management. These guidelines are accessible on the WHO website. 5. Chakravorty S and colleagues developed the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay, which enhances the detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampin resistance. This assay is suitable for point-of-care testing and was detailed in the journal mBio in 2017. 6. Camus JC and colleagues re-annotated the genome sequence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv, providing critical insights into its genetic structure. This work was published in the journal Microbiology in 2002. 7. Schünemann HJ and colleagues outlined the GRADE guidelines for assessing test accuracy, including factors such as inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias. These guidelines were published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2020. 8. Line probe assays for detecting drug-resistant tuberculosis have been developed to assist laboratory staff and clinicians in interpreting and reporting results. A guide for this purpose is available in PDF format. 9. Nathavitharana RR and colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the accuracy of line probe assays for diagnosing pulmonary and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. The findings were published in the European Respiratory Journal in 2017. 10. Rapid diagnostic tools for tuberculosis, including molecular tests, have been developed to improve detection rates. A brochure detailing these advancements was published by Hain Life Science in 2015. 11. Gikalo MB and colleagues investigated the role of eis mutations in the development of kanamycin resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates from the Moscow region. Their findings were published in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2012. 12. Bossuyt PM and colleagues updated the STARD 2015 guidelines, which provide a comprehensive list of essential items for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies. This update was published in the BMJ in 2015. 13. Sekiguchi J and colleagues developed and evaluated a line probe assay for the rapid identification of pncA mutations in pyrazinamide-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2007. 14. WHO has issued consolidated guidelines on rapid diagnostics for tuberculosis detection, emphasizing the importance of timely and accurate testing. 15. Köser CU and colleagues explored the optimal combination of genotypic and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing methods for pyrazinamide. Their findings were published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2020. 16. Groessl EJ and colleagues conducted a cost analysis of rapid diagnostics for drug-resistant tuberculosis, highlighting the economic implications of these tools. This study was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2018. 17. Li X and colleagues analyzed the impact of rapid diagnosis of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis on healthcare expenditures prior to initiating appropriate treatment. Their findings were published in Infection and Drug Resistance in 2019. 18. Pooran A and colleagues examined the costs associated with diagnosing and managing drug-resistant tuberculosis in South Africa. This study was published in PLoS One in 2013. 19. Shah M and colleagues compared the laboratory costs of rapid molecular tests with conventional diagnostics for tuberculosis and drug-resistant tuberculosis detection in South Africa. Their findings were published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2013. 20. Zignol M and colleagues conducted a multicountry surveillance project to assess population-based resistance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates to pyrazinamide and fluoroquinolones. The results were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2016. 21. Jouet A and colleagues utilized deep amplicon sequencing to predict susceptibility or resistance to 13 anti-tuberculosis drugs without the need for culture. This study was published in the European Respiratory Journal in 2021. 22. A manual for detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis nucleic acids and drug resistance genes has been developed by Hangzhou ShengTing Medical Technology Co. in China. 23. Engel N and colleagues synthesized qualitative evidence on the perspectives of recipients and providers regarding rapid molecular tests for tuberculosis and drug resistance. This synthesis was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2022. 24. WHO has published a supplementary document cataloging mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and their association with drug resistance. 25. The WHO Global TB Programme commissions systematic reviews to evaluate the performance and use of diagnostic tools and methods for tuberculosis. These reviews inform the development of evidence-based guidelines. 26. The GRADE approach is used to assess the certainty of evidence for diagnostic accuracy and other factors, such as cost-effectiveness and end-user perspectives, to inform recommendations. 27. The WHO convenes a Guideline Development Group (GDG) to review evidence and develop recommendations based on consensus or voting when necessary. 28. Recommendations are formulated using the Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework, which considers factors such as test accuracy, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, equity, and feasibility. 29. The GDG evaluates the certainty of evidence, including the accuracy of diagnostic tests, their direct benefits and harms, and their impact on patient management. 30. The acceptability and feasibility of implementing diagnostic tools are assessed, considering factors such as training needs, biosafety requirements, and turnaround time for results. 31. The WHO guidelines undergo review by an External Review Group (ERG) to ensure clarity, accuracy, and relevance before finalization. 32. The WHO emphasizes the importance of addressing serious and urgent global health problems, such as tuberculosis, through evidence-based recommendations.
